compatibility.title: Which BMW Models Use the M60B40?
compatibility.intro: The M60B40 was BMW's first production V8 in over 25 years, debuting in the E32 7 Series and quickly spreading across the range. It powered the 5 Series, 7 Series and 8 Series from 1992 to 1996, and was also used by Alpina in tuned forms.

failures.title: BMW M60B40 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Nikasil cylinder bore wear - the M60's most notorious issue
items.whatHappens: Early M60B40 engines featured Nikasil (nickel‑silicon carbide) cylinder bore coatings. In markets with high‑sulphur fuel - including the UK in the 1990s - the sulphur reacted with the Nikasil coating, causing premature bore wear and loss of compression. Symptoms include rough idle, difficult cold starting, power loss and, in severe cases, the engine failing to start. BMW addressed the issue by switching to Alusil (aluminium‑silicon alloy) bores in later production engines. Many affected engines were replaced under warranty, so most surviving M60B40s have Alusil blocks.
items.repairVsReplace: If the Nikasil bores are worn, the block is effectively scrap - the coating cannot be re‑applied economically. A replacement Alusil‑block engine is the only sensible solution. Always check the block casting before buying an M60B40.

items.title: Valley pan gasket leaks
items.whatHappens: The valley pan gasket - located under the intake manifold - degrades over time, leading to coolant and oil leaks. This is one of the most common M60 issues and can cause overheating if coolant loss is ignored.
items.repairVsReplace: The valley pan gasket is replaceable (around £300-£600 at an independent specialist). It's a labour‑intensive job due to intake manifold removal, but far cheaper than a full engine replacement.

items.title: Oil pump fasteners loosening
items.whatHappens: The oil pump casing fasteners can loosen over time, with bolts backing out and falling into the oil pan. This can lead to oil pressure loss and catastrophic engine failure.
items.repairVsReplace: Drop the oil pan and tighten the oil pump bolts - a preventative maintenance job costing around £200-£400. This should be considered essential on any M60B40 without documented evidence of the work.

variants.title: M60B40 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: The M60 family consists of two main engines: the 3.0‑litre M60B30 and the 4.0‑litre M60B40. Within the M60B40, the key distinction is the cylinder bore material - Nikasil or Alusil - rather than formal sub‑codes. INTRO: The M60B40 covers a single displacement (4.0 litres) but has important production revisions. The critical difference for buyers is the cylinder bore material, which determines long‑term viability. - Fitted to: Early E32 740i (1992-1994), early E34 540i (1993-1994), early E31 840Ci (1993-1994) - Key technical difference: Nikasil (nickel‑silicon carbide) cylinder bore coating - a high‑performance coating that proved vulnerable to high‑sulphur fuels - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Nikasil bore wear is the defining issue for these engines. If the engine has not been replaced with an Alusil block, bore wear is a significant risk. Compression and leakdown testing is essential before purchase. - Interchange note: Nikasil‑block M60B40s are fully interchangeable with Alusil‑block M60B40s - the block casting is the only difference. Many Nikasil engines were replaced under warranty with Alusil blocks. - Fitted to: Late E32 740i (1994), E38 740i (1994-1996), late E34 540i (1994-1997), late E31 840Ci (1994-1996) - Key technical difference: Alusil (aluminium‑silicon alloy) cylinder bores - a more durable material that is not vulnerable to high‑sulphur fuel - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above (valley pan gasket, oil pump bolts) but does not suffer from the Nikasil bore wear issue. This is the preferred block for replacement engines.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement M60B40 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used M60B40 makes sense only if the block is confirmed Alusil (or a Nikasil block with documented compression test results showing healthy bores). The primary risk with used units is undisclosed Nikasil bore wear - insist on a compression and leakdown test before purchase. For lower‑value E34 540i or E32 740i examples where the car itself is worth under £3,000-£4,000, a used engine with proven Alusil block can be a cost‑effective option. View used engines

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper M60B40 recon includes new valley pan gasket, valve cover gaskets, intake manifold gaskets, timing chain guides, and oil pump bolt tightening. It should also include a full inspection of the cylinder bores (confirming Alusil or healthy Nikasil) and a crankshaft inspection. This is the right call for most replacements - you get a like‑new unit with the known weak points already addressed, backed by 12-24 months warranty. View reconditioned engines

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified for high‑value, collectable or low‑mileage E31 840Ci or Alpina‑tuned cars where originality matters. An upgraded rebuild should include new timing chain components, oil pump fasteners secured with threadlock, and a full set of gaskets. For standard applications, reconditioned is usually more cost‑effective. View rebuilt engines

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: All engines can be supplied and fitted through our network of vetted UK BMW specialists - nationwide coverage with 12‑month warranty on labour and parts. View supply & fit
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The M60B40 sits in 1990s BMWs - E34 540i (£2,000-£8,000), E32/E38 740i (£1,500-£6,000), E31 840Ci (£5,000-£20,000+ for good examples). A £3,500-£5,500 reconditioned engine plus £1,000-£1,500 fitting is a significant investment - for lower‑value examples (sub‑£4,000 540i or 740i), a used Alusil‑block engine may be the more economic choice. For collectable 840Ci or low‑mileage examples, the investment is usually justified by the car's value and rarity. Always evaluate the whole‑vehicle condition before committing.

items.question: What are the common problems with the BMW M60B40 engine?
items.answer: The M60B40's most critical issue is Nikasil cylinder bore wear - early engines (1992-1994) with Nikasil coatings can suffer bore wear from high-sulphur fuel, leading to compression loss. Other common issues include valley pan gasket leaks (coolant/oil) and oil pump fasteners that can loosen over time. Nikasil wear is the main concern; Alusil blocks are the preferred option. Valley pan gasket replacement costs £300-£600. Oil pump bolt tightening is essential preventative maintenance.

items.answer: A used M60B40 is only worth considering if the block is confirmed Alusil (or a Nikasil block with documented compression test results showing healthy bores). A reconditioned unit is safer, as it includes new valley pan gasket, timing chain guides and gaskets with 12-24 months warranty, typically costing £3,500-£5,500 supply-only. Used engines risk undisclosed Nikasil bore wear. Alusil blocks are the preferred option for long-term reliability. Compression and leakdown testing is essential before purchase.

items.question: How do I know if my BMW has the M60B40 engine?
items.answer: The M60B40 is stamped on the engine block - look for "M60B40" or "408S1" on the identification plate on the left-hand side of the engine. You can also decode your VIN - BMW models with M60B40 show this engine code in parts systems. Enter your registration above for confirmation. The V5C logbook lists the engine number. Check the block casting to confirm Nikasil or Alusil. Alusil blocks are preferred for reliability.

items.question: Is the M60B40 a reliable engine?
items.answer: The M60B40 is generally considered robust and reliable - many examples have exceeded 400,000 miles with proper maintenance. The non-VANOS design is a reliability advantage, as there are no VANOS seals or solenoids to fail. However, early Nikasil engines are vulnerable to bore wear, so an Alusil-block engine is strongly recommended for long-term ownership. Alusil-block engines are the most reliable. Regular oil changes and maintenance are essential. Oil pump bolt tightening is a critical preventative job.
